newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG mercenaries were there to fight, contract says.
newsitem.headline: PNG mercenaries were there to fight, contract says.

text.p: Mercenaries hired by the Papua New Guinea government to help put down a rebellion on Bougainville island would have been frontline fighters, not just mere consultants, according to their contract.

The "strictly confidential" contract between the South Pacific nation and British-based mercenary firm Sandline International was handed to journalists on Thursday by the sacked army commander who sparked PNG's crisis.

And it showed that the South African veterans led by former British colonel Tim Spicer were not hired just to train troops but to conduct "offensive operations" to quell the Bougainville uprising and recapture a vast copper mine on the island.

More than 50 of the mercenaries were due to fly out of PNG on Friday, Australian media reported. It was not clear if Spicer, a former United Nations peacekeeper and spokesman in Bosnia, would be allowed to leave with them.
Their US$36 million operation was thwarted by Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok, the army commander sacked after turning against Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan on Monday.
Singirok has been holed up inside Port Moresby's main Murray barracks throughout the crisis, briefing reporters in his backyard overlooking the Pacific ocean.
On Friday, he gave them a copy of the 10-page legal contract outlining the mercenaries' task.

Signed by Deputy Prime Minister Chris Haiveta and Spicer, the contract stipulates the mercenaries would "conduct offensive operations in Bougainville in conjunction with PNG defence forces to render the (Bougainville Revolutionary Army) militarily ineffective and repossess the Panguna mine".
Internationally condemned for hiring the mercenaries, Chan had said they would only be used to train PNG troops and would go to Bougainville only as consultants.
The contract states the mercenaries would be employed for an initial period of three months or until the BRA were defeated.
Fifty percent of the fee was to be paid when the contract was signed on January 31, with the remaining $18 million to be paid within 30 days of deployment.
An appendix at the back of the contract breaks down costs into $29 million for equipment and $7 million for manpower.
A 45-strong "special forces team" was costed at $4.5 million -- or $100,000 per soldier. PNG soldiers earn around $40 a week.
Sandline, whose operatives would be called "Special Constables" would also provide "strategic and operational briefings" to the prime minister, defence minister and defence force commander.
The mercenaries, numbering almost 70, began leaving on Wednesday. The last group, of around 55 including Spicer, left Friday on a chartered flight for Hong Kong.
The nine-year secessionist rebellion on Bougainville began when landowners demanding compensation for mine works began attacking buses carrying miners.
The Panguna mine, one of the three largest in the world, was shut down in 1989. It is controlled by the Anglo-Australian company RTZ-CRA, the world's biggest mining group.

Thwarted by the soldiers they were meant to serve, the mercenaries never reached Bougainville. Spicer -- who signed his contract "Tim Spicer OBE" or Order of the British Empire -- and his South African soldiers of fortune never had a chance to fulfill their contract.
